name: elfx86exts
desc: Decodes x86 binaries (ELF and Mach-O) and prints out ISA extensions in use
why: Reveals which x86 instruction set extensions a binary actually uses, a neat way to peer into what a compiled program does.

brief.what_it_is: elfx86exts is a command-line tool that disassembles a compiled binary and prints out which instruction set extensions the code uses. It reads ELF and Mach-O binaries (the changelog also mentions PE/Windows support) and disassembles them with the Capstone engine. It picks the x86/x86-64 or ARM64 analysis path automatically from the binary's CPU architecture, and exits if the architecture is neither. Per the 0.3.0 changelog, it also prints a best guess at the minimum Intel CPU generation needed to run the binary. The README shows no sample output, so the exact output format is unverified.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes a tool that answers which instruction set extensions a binary actually uses, and the author's own tone is loose about it ('I have no idea what I'm doing here, but it seems to work').
brief.how_it_works: The tool parses the executable's container format, then disassembles it with the Capstone disassembly engine, one instruction at a time per the 0.6.2 changelog (an earlier bulk approach used too much memory). It then checks the decoded instructions against extension families and reports the ones seen. The README does not spell out the matching table in detail, though the changelog mentions an internal table of which extensions arrived in which CPU model.

brief.install_notes: Requires a Rust toolchain and the Capstone disassembly engine C library, both available through common package managers. Then run 'cargo install elfx86exts'; the README says --force is needed to upgrade between versions. Prepackaged builds exist on the Arch Linux AUR and on conda-forge (Linux only at the time of the README). No accounts, hardware, or first-run configuration are mentioned. Homebrew is not mentioned in the README.
brief.standout: The project name is a deliberate joke: the README and changelog keep noting that it now handles far more than the name suggests (ELF, Mach-O, PE, and ARM64). It also estimates the minimum Intel CPU generation a binary needs, which is a practical angle beyond a plain instruction-list dump.
brief.status: Maintained at a low tempo. The changelog's latest entry is elfx86exts 0.6.2, dated 2023-10-22, preceded by 0.6.1 (2023-10-21) and 0.6.0 (2023-10-12). I did not see a later release or a commit date, so I cannot confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: ARM64 support is described as preliminary. conda-forge packaging is Linux only. Building from source needs a Rust toolchain and Capstone. The README has no usage section, so flags and output format are unknown from these sources. The author describes the work with self-deprecating hedges, so do not present it as a polished or authoritative analysis tool. Licensed under MIT.
